title: The role of retained austenite stability in determining yield strength of a quenching and partitioning processed medium-Mn steel
abstract: Quenching and partitioning (Q&P) steels, typically composed of martensite and retained austenite, exhibit an excellent combination of tensile strength and ductility. However, their yield strength is relatively low, and the underlying mechanism remains controversial. In this study, a medium-Mn steel was processed via a quenching-tempering and partitioning route. The experimental steel underwent quenching to room temperature retaining 8.1 vol% of austenite, followed by tempering within the range of 150∼300 °C. With the increase of tempering temperature, the yield strengths of the specimens elevate from 540 MPa to 980 MPa and the C contents increase from 0.40 wt% to 0.84 wt%. Tensile tests conducted at different temperatures and in-situ electron backscatter diffraction (in-situ EBSD) analysis clarify that stress-assisted martensitic transformation of retained austenite occurs during the yielding stage, donating macroscopic yielding. By increasing the C concentration in austenite through tempering, the austenite mechanical stability is raised, thereby enhancing the macroscopic yield strength. This work provides a theoretical foundation for the design of high-yield-strength martensitic steels with retained austenite.
